claim: WRN was identified as a potential selective dependency in a subset of 398 cancer cell models in Project DRIVE pooled shRNA viability screen.
source: WRN was identified as a potential selective dependency in a subset of 398 cancer cell models in a recent pooled shRNA viability screen covering approximately 8000 genes (Project DRIVE) (https://oncologynibr.shinyapps.io/drive/; McDonald et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the Project DRIVE study (McDonald et al., 2017) and reference to the screening data.

claim: Depletion of WRN exclusively affects viability of a subset of CRC, gastric and endometrial cancer cell models with RSA sensitivity scores ≤−3.
source: Depletion of WRN exclusively affects viability of a subset of CRC, gastric and endometrial cancer cell models reflected by RSA (redundant siRNA activity) sensitivity scores ≤−3, indicative of cell essentiality (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and the RSA scoring methodology from the screening study.

claim: CRC, gastric and endometrial cancers are the three human malignancies with the highest frequency of MSI-H status.
source: Intriguingly, CRC, gastric and endometrial cancers are the three human malignancies with the highest frequency of MSI-H status (Cortes-Ciriano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cortes-Ciriano et al., 2017.

claim: A Random Forest model classifies WRN sensitive and insensitive cell lines with an accuracy of 0.89 and a recall rate for sensitive lines of 0.69.
source: This model classifies WRN sensitive and insensitive cell lines with an accuracy of 0.89 and a recall rate for sensitive lines of 0.69.
evidence: The claim is supported by the results of the Random Forest modeling analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: MLH1 expression is the feature most highly associated with WRN dependency classification outcome.
source: An analysis of variable importance revealed MLH1 expression as the feature most highly associated with the classification outcome, in line with the frequent inactivation of the MLH1 gene in MSI-H CRC (Cunningham et al., 1998; Herman et al., 1998; Kane et al., 1997; Kuismanen et al., 2000) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the Random Forest variable importance analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citations to studies on MLH1 inactivation.

claim: WRN dependency anti-correlates with MLH1 mRNA expression levels among cell models used in Project DRIVE (p=1.02*10−4).
source: Consistently, WRN dependency anti-correlates with MLH1 mRNA expression levels among the cell models used in Project DRIVE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; p=1.02*10−4, Fisher's exact test, stratification of MLH1-low and -high expressing cell models according to median MLH1 expression [TPM 37.44]).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test) and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WRN dependency is strongly associated with MSI-H status across CRC, gastric and endometrial models (p=4.91*10−8).
source: Analysis of gene dependency and MSS/MSI-H status data revealed that WRN dependency was strongly associated with MSI-H status across CRC, gastric and endometrial models (p=4.91*10−8, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test) of gene dependency and MSI status data.

claim: Of the 18 cell lines classified as MSI-H, 15 cell lines (83%) were sensitive to WRN depletion using an RSA value of ≤−3.
source: Of the 18 cell lines classified as MSI-H, 15 cell lines (83%) were sensitive to WRN depletion using an RSA value of ≤−3 to define WRN dependency (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of the screening data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: WRN is dispensable for viability in all MSS cell models.
source: In contrast, WRN is dispensable for viability in all MSS cell models (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MSI-H status is a strong predictor for WRN sensitivity of cancer cells.
source: Our analysis suggests that MSI-H status is a strong predictor for WRN sensitivity of cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the statistical associations and experimental data presented.

claim: WRN depletion using siRNA profoundly affected viability in MSI-H CRC models (HCT 116, RKO, SNU-C4) but not in MSS CRC models (SK-CO-1, CaCo-2, SW480).
source: In agreement with the results from Project DRIVE, WRN depletion using a mixture of four siRNA duplexes (Pool) or an individual siRNA (#1) targeting WRN profoundly affected viability in MSI-H, but not in MSS CRC models (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental viability data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Depletion of PLK1 had a detrimental effect on viability of both MSS and MSI-H cell lines.
source: In contrast, depletion of the known essential mitotic kinase PLK1, had a detrimental effect on viability of both MSS and MSI-H cell lines.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental viability data comparing PLK1 and WRN depletion effects.

claim: WRN knock-down impaired viability of three MSI-H endometrial carcinoma cell lines (HEC-265, ISHIKAWA, HEC-6) but not the MSS cell line MFE-280.
source: Likewise, we observed that WRN knock-down impaired viability of three MSI-H endometrial carcinoma cells lines (HEC-265, ISHIKAWA, HEC-6), but not the MSS cell line MFE-280 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental viability data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Non-transformed hTERT RPE-1 cells did not display sensitivity to knock-down of WRN.
source: Similar to MSS cancer models, non-transformed telomerase-immortalized human retinal pigment epithelial cells (hTERT RPE-1) did not display sensitivity to knock-down of WRN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental viability data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Depletion of BLM significantly impaired viability of hTERT RPE-1 but not HCT 116 cells.
source: It is noteworthy, that the depletion of the related RecQ helicase BLM significantly impaired viability of hTERT RPE-1, but not HCT 116 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental viability data comparing BLM depletion effects in different cell lines.

claim: WRN/p53 co-depletion exacerbated the reduction in viability compared to WRN knock-down alone in HCT 116 cells.
source: However, WRN/p53 co-depletion exacerbated the reduction in viability compared to WRN knock-down alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental viability data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A slight elevation of p53 protein levels was observed upon WRN depletion in both HCT 116 and SK-CO-1 cell lines.
source: Interestingly, in both cell lines we observed a slight elevation of p53 protein levels upon WRN depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Reconstitution of MLH1 and MSH3 in HCT 116 cells resulted in only a modest increase of viability upon WRN knock-down compared to parental cells.
source: In both HCT 116 +ch3 and HCT 116 +ch3+ch5 cell lines, we noticed only a modest increase of viability upon WRN knock-down compared to the parental cells or the HCT 116 +ch2 control line (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) despite equally potent WRN knock-down in all models (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental viability data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: Single or concomitant knockdown of MLH1 and MSH3 did not affect cell viability of WRN-deficient SW480 cell lines.
source: We did not observe an effect of either single or concomitant knockdown of MLH1 and MSH3 on cell viability of the WRN-deficient SW480 cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), despite efficacious depletion of the mRNAs encoding MLH1 and MSH3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental viability data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claim: WRN dependence of MSI-H cancer cell lines might not be attributable to an acute and hard-wired synthetic lethal interaction between WRN and MLH1/MSH3.
source: These results suggest that WRN dependence of MSI-H cancer cell lines might not be attributable to an acute and hard-wired synthetic lethal interaction between WRN and MLH1/MSH3.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the reconstitution and depletion experimental results.

claim: MSI-H HCT 116 cells expressing WRN sgRNAs depleted to a similar level as observed for the RPA3 positive control.
source: In contrast, MSI-H HCT 116 cells expressing WRN sgRNAs depleted to a similar level as observed for the RPA3 positive control.
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR-Cas9 depletion assay data.

claim: sgRNAs directed against the exonuclease, helicase and RQC domains of WRN were most effective in depleting MSI-H cells.
source: sgRNAs directed against the exonuclease, helicase and RQC domains were most effective, implying a functional or structural requirement of both these domains in the context of WRN dependency.
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR domain scanning data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Strong depletion effects were observed for sgRNAs targeting the C-terminal HTH motif of WRN.
source: Interestingly, strong depletion effects were also observed for sgRNAs targeting the C-terminal HTH motif (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR domain scanning data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: WRN depletion did not affect viability in MSS CRC cell line HT-29.
source: We did not observe depletion of cells harboring WRN targeting sgRNAs in the MSS CRC cell line HT-29.
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR-Cas9 depletion assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Wild-type WRNr expression was sufficient to render HCT 116 cells inert to knock-down of endogenous WRN.
source: Importantly, both the high and low expression level of wild-type WRNr was sufficient to render HCT 116 cells inert to knock-down of endogenous WRN (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Exogenous expression of the nuclease-dead form of WRNr almost completely rescued the effect of endogenous WRN depletion.
source: Exogenous expression of the nuclease-dead form of WRNr almost completely rescued the effect of endogenous WRN depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Both the ATP-binding deficient and double-mutant form of WRNr were unable to restore viability following depletion of endogenous WRN.
source: In stark contrast, although expressed at similar or higher levels than WRNr wild-type, both the ATP-binding deficient and double-mutant form of WRNr were unable to restore viability following depletion of endogenous WRN (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ATP-binding activity of WRN and possibly its helicase function are crucial for the survival of MSI-H CRC cells.
source: In summary, these results indicate that the ATP-binding activity of WRN and possibly its helicase function are crucial for the survival of MSI-H CRC cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the rescue experiments with WRN mutants.

claim: WRN depletion in MSI-H HCT 116 and RKO cells resulted in formation of chromatin bridges and micronuclei.
source: Strikingly, in HCT 116 and RKO cells we observed formation of chromatin bridges and micronuclei upon WRN knock-down, both potential consequences of failed sister genome partitioning during mitosis (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Enlarged nuclei, indicative of failed mitosis, were observed upon WRN knock-down in HCT 116 cells.
source: Enlarged nuclei, indicative of failed mitosis, were additionally observed upon WRN knock-down in HCT 116 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence observations.

claim: WRN depletion did not affect baseline levels of chromatin bridges and micronuclei in MSS CRC cancer models SK-CO-1 and SW480.
source: Quantification of the frequency of chromatin bridges and micronuclei revealed that WRN depletion did not affect baseline levels of these aberrant nuclear morphologies in the MSS CRC cancer models SK-CO-1 and SW480, while the frequency of both chromatin bridges and micronuclei was strongly increased upon WRN knock-down in the MSI-H CRC cell lines HCT 116 and RKO (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: WRN depletion led to a slight increase of chromatin bridge and micronucleus formation in hTERT RPE-1 cells, although far less pronounced compared to MSI-H CRC models.
source: In non-transformed hTERT RPE-1 cells, WRN depletion led to a slight increase of chromatin bridge and micronucleus formation, although far less pronounced compared to the MSI-H CRC models (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Live cell imaging revealed a strong increase of the incidence of lagging chromosomes and chromosome bridges during mitosis in WRN-depleted MSI-H CRC cell lines HCT 116 and RKO, but not in MSS SW480 cells.
source: Supportive of the immunofluorescence studies, live cell imaging revealed a strong increase of the incidence of lagging chromosomes and chromosome bridges during mitosis in WRN-depleted MSI-H CRC cell lines HCT 116 and RKO, but not in MSS SW480 cells (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: WRN depletion in MSI-H cells results in nuclear morphology and integrity aberrations that are manifested during cell division.
source: We conclude that WRN depletion in MSI-H cells results in nuclear morphology and integrity aberrations that are manifested during cell division.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the immunofluorescence and live cell imaging data.

claim: Nuclear abnormalities are causally linked to the anti-proliferative effect of WRN loss in MSI-H models.
source: The correlation of these defects with the observed cell viability reduction in MSI-H models suggests that nuclear abnormalities are causally linked to the anti-proliferative effect of WRN loss.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation between nuclear defects and viability reduction.

claim: WRN loss elicited structural chromosome aberrations, such as chromosome breaks and non-homologous radial formations, in MSI-H CRC cell lines HCT 116 and RKO.
source: Strikingly, WRN loss elicited structural chromosome aberrations, such as chromosome breaks and non-homologous radial formations, in the MSI-H CRC cell lines HCT 116 and RKO (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by chromosome spread analysis data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: WRN depletion resulted in a strong increase in the fraction of cells harboring 1–5 or >5 chromosome breaks in two MSI-H CRC models.
source: Quantification of the number of chromatin breaks per karyotype demonstrated a strong increase in the fraction of cells harboring 1–5 or >5 chromosome breaks in the two MSI-H CRC models upon WRN depletion (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative chromosome spread analysis data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In MSS CRC model SW480 and hTERT RPE-1 non-transformed cells only a minor increase of karyotypes with chromosome breaks was detected upon WRN depletion.
source: In the MSS CRC model SW480 and hTERT RPE-1 non-transformed cells only a minor increase of karyotypes with chromosome breaks was detected (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative chromosome spread analysis data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A strong induction of γ-H2AX was observed upon siRNA-mediated depletion of WRN in MSI-H, but not MSS, CRC cancer cell lines.
source: We observed a strong induction of γ-H2AX upon siRNA-mediated depletion of WRN in MSI-H, but not MSS, CRC cancer cell lines (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In both HCT 116 and RKO MSI-H CRC lines, WRN depletion led to an increase in nuclear γ-H2AX signal similar to or higher than upon treatment with etoposide.
source: Strikingly, in both HCT 116 and RKO MSI-H CRC lines, WRN depletion led to an increase in nuclear γ-H2AX signal similar to or higher than upon treatment of cells with the DNA double-strand break-inducing agent etoposide (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Nuclear γ-H2AX levels in hTERT RPE-1 cells were strongly increased by treatment with etoposide, while loss of WRN had no effect.
source: Importantly, nuclear γ-H2AX levels in non-transformed and MSS hTERT RPE-1 cells were strongly increased by treatment with etoposide, while loss of WRN had no effect in this model (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WRN helicase is essential for maintaining genome integrity in MSI-H cells by preventing chromosome breaks and erroneous chromosome fusions.
source: Our analyses suggest that WRN helicase is essential for maintaining genome integrity in MSI-H cells by preventing chromosome breaks and erroneous chromosome fusions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the chromosome aberration data.

claim: The detection of DNA damage markers in interphase nuclei of WRN-depleted MSI-H cells suggests that mitotic and post-mitotic aberrations originate from genome integrity defects in interphase.
source: The detection of DNA damage markers in interphase nuclei of WRN-depleted MSI-H cells suggests that the aforementioned mitotic and post-mitotic aberrations originate from genome integrity defects in interphase.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the γ-H2AX immunofluorescence data.

claim: Genome integrity defects are responsible for the profound reduction in viability of MSI-H cancer cells upon WRN loss.
source: The correlation of chromosome aberrations and nuclear abnormalities with MSI-H status following loss of WRN function indicate that genome integrity defects are responsible for the profound reduction in viability of MSI-H cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation between genome integrity defects and viability reduction.

claim: Pembrolizumab, nivolumab and ipilimumab have been approved for targeting PD-1 and CTLA-4 in MSI-H tumors.
source: Treatment paradigms for MSI-H tumors have recently shifted with the approval of the immune checkpoint agents pembrolizumab, nivolumab and ipilimumab, targeting programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated Protein 4 (CTLA-4) in this patient segment (Le et al., 2017; Le et al., 2015; Overman et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical studies (Le et al., 2017; Le et al., 2015; Overman et al., 2018).

claim: Pembrolizumab constitutes the first cancer therapy approval based on a patient selection biomarker irrespective of the tumor type.
source: Pembrolizumab constitutes the first cancer therapy approval based on a patient selection biomarker irrespective of the tumor type, highlighting MSI-H status as a therapeutically trackable and clinically implemented feature of tumor cells (Goswami and Sharma, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Goswami and Sharma, 2017.

claim: Intrinsic and acquired resistance to immunotherapy represents a continuous medical need in MSI-H cancer.
source: While responses to immune checkpoint blockade in MSI-H cancer are often durable, intrinsic and acquired resistance to immunotherapy represents a continuous medical need in MSI-H cancer.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about immunotherapy resistance.

claim: MSI-H status is linked to a CpG island methylator (CIMP) phenotype and an increased mutational burden.
source: However, while MSI-H status is linked to a CpG island methylator (CIMP) phenotype and an increased mutational burden, a functional dependency enabling selective targeting of MSI-H cancer cells remains elusive.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about MSI-H tumors.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of WRN helicase function represents an opportunity to develop a novel targeted therapy for MSI-H cancers.
source: Our study suggests that pharmacological inhibition of WRN helicase function represents an opportunity to develop a novel targeted therapy for MSI-H cancers.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the study findings and represents speculation about therapeutic potential.

claim: MMR deficiency and MSI-H status represent a genetic determinant for WRN dependency regardless of tumor type.
source: Our data suggest that similar to the tumor agnostic activity of checkpoint blockade, MMR deficiency and MSI-H status represent a genetic determinant for WRN dependency regardless of tumor type.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data showing WRN dependency across multiple MSI-H tumor types.

claim: The genetic interaction of WRN and MMR genes seems to be distinct from acute and hard-wired synthetic lethal interactions.
source: As indicated by the MLH1/MSH3 reconstitution and depletion studies, the genetic interaction of WRN and MMR genes cannot readily be recapitulated using isogenic cell models and thus seems to be distinct from acute and hard-wired synthetic lethal interactions, such as described in cancer cells for the alternate BAF complex ATPases SMARCA2/SMARCA4 or the cohesin subunits STAG1/STAG2 (Oike et al., 2013; van der Lelij et al., 2017; Benedetti et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the reconstitution/depletion experiments and comparison to known synthetic lethal interactions.

claim: WRN is a member of the RecQ DNA helicase subfamily.
source: Werner syndrome helicase (WRN) is a member of the RecQ DNA helicase subfamily (Croteau et al., 2014; Yu et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Croteau et al., 2014 and Yu et al., 1996.

claim: RecQ helicases are involved in multiple DNA processing steps including DNA replication, double-strand break repair, transcription and telomere maintenance.
source: RecQ helicases are involved in multiple DNA processing steps including DNA replication, double-strand break repair, transcription and telomere maintenance and are therefore considered to serve as 'genome caretakers' (Chu and Hickson, 2009; Croteau et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chu and Hickson, 2009 and Croteau et al., 2014.

claim: Defects in WRN, BLM and RECQL4 give rise to human disease syndromes associated with developmental defects and cancer predisposition.
source: The critical function of this protein family in genome maintenance is underscored by the fact that defects in three of the five family members – WRN, Bloom Syndrome RecQ Like Helicase (BLM) and RecQ Like Helicase 4 (RECQL4) – give rise to human disease syndromes associated with developmental defects and cancer predisposition (Brosh, 2013; Oshima et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brosh, 2013 and Oshima et al., 2017.

claim: Patients with Werner syndrome display a premature ageing phenotype including arteriosclerosis, type II diabetes and osteoporosis.
source: Specifically, patients with Werner syndrome display a premature ageing phenotype including arteriosclerosis, type II diabetes and osteoporosis and are prone to develop tumors of mesenchymal origin, such as soft tissue sarcoma or osteosarcoma (Goto et al., 2013; Hickson, 2003; Lauper et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Goto et al., 2013; Hickson, 2003; and Lauper et al., 2013.

claim: WRN is unique among RecQ family helicases in possessing 3'−5' exonuclease activity.
source: WRN is unique among RecQ family helicases in possessing 3'−5' exonuclease activity (Huang et al., 1998; Kamath-Loeb et al., 1998; Shen et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 1998; Kamath-Loeb et al., 1998; and Shen et al., 1998.

claim: Defects in components of the DNA repair machinery are a common characteristic of tumor cells.
source: Defects in components of the DNA repair machinery, such as BRCA1/2 mutations or impaired DNA mismatch repair (MMR), are a common characteristic of tumor cells, accelerating the accumulation of DNA mutations or chromosomal aberrations that are required for neoplastic growth and transformation (Kinzler and Vogelstein, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kinzler and Vogelstein, 1997.

claim: PARP inhibitors are the first clinically approved drugs exploiting synthetic lethality for therapy of BRCA1/BRCA2-deficient tumors.
source: The first clinically approved drugs exploiting such a SL interaction are Poly(ADP-Ribose) Polymerase (PARP) inhibitors for therapy of BRCA1/BRCA2-deficient tumors (Kaufman et al., 2015; Lord and Ashworth, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kaufman et al., 2015 and Lord and Ashworth, 2017.

claim: MMR deficiency is caused by inactivation of genes involved in the resolution of nucleotide base-base mismatches during DNA replication.
source: MMR deficiency is caused by inactivation of genes of the DNA repair machinery involved in the resolution of nucleotide base-base mismatches during DNA replication (Jiricny, 2006; Kunkel and Erie, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jiricny, 2006 and Kunkel and Erie, 2015.

claim: MMR defects lead to characteristic variations in the length of tandem nucleotide repeats across the genome, known as microsatellite instability (MSI).
source: MMR defects lead to characteristic variations in the length of tandem nucleotide repeats across the genome, known as microsatellite instability (MSI) (Ellegren, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ellegren, 2004.

claim: Germline mutations in MMR genes are causative for Lynch syndrome, a cancer predisposition condition.
source: Germline mutations in MMR genes, most commonly MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2, are causative for Lynch syndrome, a cancer predisposition condition associated with increased lifetime risk to develop colorectal cancer (CRC) or other tumor types including endometrial and gastric carcinoma (Hampel et al., 2005; Lynch and Krush, 1971; Lynch et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hampel et al., 2005; Lynch and Krush, 1971; and Lynch et al., 2015.

claim: In sporadic CRC, MSI is frequently observed due to epigenetic silencing of MLH1.
source: In sporadic, nonhereditary CRC, MSI is frequently observed due to epigenetic silencing of MLH1 (Cunningham et al., 1998; Herman et al., 1998; Kane et al., 1997; Kuismanen et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cunningham et al., 1998; Herman et al., 1998; Kane et al., 1997; and Kuismanen et al., 2000.

claim: MSI-H tumors display a hypermutator phenotype.
source: MSI-high (MSI-H) tumors display a hypermutator phenotype (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012), which entails increased immunogenicity, amendable to therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors (Le et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012.

claim: Targeted therapies directly exploiting the MMR-deficient status of tumor cells do not exist.
source: However, targeted therapies directly exploiting the MMR-deficient status of tumor cells do not exist.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the current therapeutic landscape.

claim: WRN loss-of-function causes mitotic defects and nuclear abnormalities in MSI-H cells.
source: Loss of WRN causes mitotic defects and nuclear abnormalities in MSI-H cells
evidence: This is a section heading that summarizes experimental findings presented in the section.

claim: WRN depletion in MSI-H cells results in structural chromosome aberrations.
source: Structural chromosome aberrations in MSI-H cells after WRN loss-of-function
evidence: This is a section heading that summarizes experimental findings presented in the section.

claim: WRN inactivation selectively impairs the viability of MSI-H but not MSS colorectal and endometrial cancer cell lines.
source: We demonstrate that WRN inactivation selectively impairs the viability of MSI-H but not microsatellite stable (MSS) colorectal and endometrial cancer cell lines.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: In MSI-H cells, WRN loss results in severe genome integrity defects.
source: In MSI-H cells, WRN loss results in severe genome integrity defects.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by chromosome spread and immunofluorescence data.

claim: ATP-binding deficient variants of WRN fail to rescue the viability phenotype of WRN-depleted MSI-H cancer cells.
source: ATP-binding deficient variants of WRN fail to rescue the viability phenotype of WRN-depleted MSI-H cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 4.

claim: WRN dependence might arise during sustained MMR-deficiency rather than from acute loss of MMR gene function.
source: Reconstitution and depletion studies indicate that WRN dependence is not attributable to acute loss of MMR gene function but might arise during sustained MMR-deficiency.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the MLH1/MSH3 reconstitution and depletion experiments.

claim: Homozygous Wrn-null mice display no overt phenotype and do not recapitulate Werner syndrome unless crossed into a Terc-null background.
source: Interestingly, homozygous Wrn-null mice display no overt phenotype and do not recapitulate the premature ageing or cancer predisposition conditions of Werner syndrome, unless crossed into a Terc-null background (Chang et al., 2004; Lebel and Leder, 1998; Lombard et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chang et al., 2004; Lebel and Leder, 1998; and Lombard et al., 2000.

claim: Mutations in Werner syndrome are almost exclusively truncating nonsense, splicing or frameshift mutations affecting WRN nuclear localization.
source: Mutations in Werner syndrome are almost exclusively truncating nonsense, splicing or frameshift mutations affecting WRN nuclear localization, suggesting that concomitant loss of WRN helicase and exonuclease function might be required for the onset of Werner syndrome (Fu et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2006; Matsumoto et al., 1997; Yokote et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2006; Matsumoto et al., 1997; and Yokote et al., 2017.

claim: Inhibition of WRN helicase function might have a therapeutic index for the treatment of MSI-H cancer without inducing Werner syndrome related phenotypes.
source: This indicates that inhibition of WRN helicase function might have a therapeutic index for the treatment of MSI-H cancer without inducing Werner syndrome related phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the mutation patterns in Werner syndrome and the rescue experiments.

claim: It is possible to develop potent and selective small molecule inhibitors of WRN helicase.
source: Given the possibility to develop potent and selective small molecule inhibitors of WRN helicase (Aggarwal et al., 2013; Aggarwal et al., 2011; Rosenthal et al., 2010), our findings outline a novel strategy for the treatment of a clinically defined subset of patients harboring MSI-H/MMR-deficient tumors.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aggarwal et al., 2013; Aggarwal et al., 2011; and Rosenthal et al., 2010.

claim: Genome instability can elicit cytoplasmic nucleic acid sensor pathways and innate immune responses.
source: Since genome instability can elicit cytoplasmic nucleic acid sensor pathways and innate immune responses (Mackenzie et al., 2017), the induction of cancer cell selective nuclear aberrations by WRN inactivation could provide a synergistic combination option with the approved immunotherapy agents for the benefit of MSI-H cancer patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mackenzie et al., 2017.

claim: WRN inactivation could provide a synergistic combination option with approved immunotherapy agents for MSI-H cancer patients.
source: Since genome instability can elicit cytoplasmic nucleic acid sensor pathways and innate immune responses (Mackenzie et al., 2017), the induction of cancer cell selective nuclear aberrations by WRN inactivation could provide a synergistic combination option with the approved immunotherapy agents for the benefit of MSI-H cancer patients.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the potential for WRN inactivation to induce immune responses.

claim: MMR activity is required for activation of the G2/M checkpoint in response to DNA damage prior to entry into mitosis.
source: MMR activity is required for activation of the G2/M checkpoint in response to DNA damage prior to entry into mitosis (O'Brien and Brown, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to O'Brien and Brown, 2006.

claim: WRN function in MSI-H cells might be critical for the resolution of DNA damage events and to prevent premature entry into mitosis.
source: WRN function in MSI-H cells might therefore be critical for the resolution of DNA damage events and to prevent premature entry into mitosis.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observed phenotypes and known functions of WRN and MMR.

claim: Cell lines derived from Werner syndrome patients display defective mitotic recombination and are susceptible to genome instability.
source: Of note, cell lines derived from Werner syndrome patients display defective mitotic recombination and are susceptible to genome instability (Prince et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Prince et al., 2001.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of WRN might allow for an MSI-H cancer-directed therapy that spares normal cells and tissues.
source: However, in MSS cancer and non-transformed cells WRN depletion had no or very mild effects on viability, suggesting that pharmacological inhibition of WRN might allow for an MSI-H cancer-directed therapy that spares normal cells and tissues.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the selective effects of WRN depletion in MSI-H versus MSS and non-transformed cells.
